label: g1_ledger
name: Router-lookahead expert prefetch
mech: A small on-die predictor reads each layer's hidden state and predicts the next layer's top-k experts one to two layers ahead. It then issues DMA from LPDDR5X into SRAM, while frequency counters keep hot experts pinned in SRAM. The closest earlier attempts are Pre-gated MoE and MoE-Infinity, which were stalled by PCIe offload at about 64 GB/s; on-package LPDDR at about 2 TB/s removes that link. The deciding quantity is the prediction hit rate multiplied by lead time, set against the per-expert fetch time; it needs at least 85% hits.
value: Frontier MoE models can be served from about $5/GB DRAM instead of HBM, with no CoWoS allocation needed.

label: g1_ledger
name: Bandwidth-by-count LPDDR decode
mech: Nine dies, each with 24 LPDDR5X packages (about 2 TB/s and 768 GB each), hold one tensor-parallel shard of a 70B FP8 model plus its KV slice. Each die streams 7.8 GB per token through double-buffered SRAM, for about 256 tok/s/user. The closest earlier attempt is Groq, whose chip count (576) was set by SRAM capacity; here capacity is DRAM, so the count is set by bandwidth alone. The deciding quantity is the SRAM reuse ratio, which must be at least about 6 to beat HBM on dollars per GB/s.
value: It delivers SRAM-dataflow-class latency with about 60× fewer chips and no HBM or CoWoS dependency.

label: g1_ledger
name: HBM-free SRAM-tiled training chip
mech: A 256 MB SRAM tile buffer feeds about 4 PFLOPS FP8 GEMMs at about 5,000 FLOP/byte. Weights, activation checkpoints and optimizer state (16 B/param) sit in LPDDR or CXL DRAM at about 2 TB/s, with hardware-sequenced prefetch. The closest earlier attempts are Dojo and Graphcore, which had SRAM only and no capacity tier, and ZeRO-Infinity, which was PCIe-bound. The deciding quantity is the achieved FLOP/byte on attention and collectives, which must stay above 2,000.
value: It cuts the HBM share of accelerator-package cost in training clusters while staying above 40% MFU.

label: g1_neg
name: Read-refreshed stacked weight DRAM
mech: Commodity-density DRAM layers are hybrid-bonded over an N3 compute die and hold only the model weights. Every decode token streams all weights in about 1 ms, and each read restores the cell. That makes refresh unnecessary even at about 105 °C, where cells lose charge too fast for normal refresh. The closest earlier attempts are HBM-PIM and AiM, which were stopped by DRAM-process logic. Here the logic stays on a logic wafer. The deciding quantity is worst-cell retention at junction temperature versus the weight sweep period. Idle chips fall back to normal refresh.
value: About 120 GB at about 100 TB/s on one die, so a 70B model decodes at more than 1,000 tok/s/user without a 576-chip SRAM farm.

label: g1_neg
name: DRAM-wafer on wafer-scale engine
mech: A full DRAM wafer is bonded wafer-on-wafer onto a wafer-scale dataflow compute wafer. Each layer adds about 1.7 TB, against 44 GB of SRAM on Cerebras WSE-3. Defects are repaired through DRAM row and column redundancy plus spare compute tiles. The closest earlier attempt is Cerebras, which was stopped by capacity and needed external MemoryX streaming. The estimated power density of about 0.5 W/mm² is gentle enough for DRAM. The deciding quantity is the yield of the bonded stack after repair.
value: A trillion-parameter FP8 model resident on one wafer at PB/s-class bandwidth, cutting the dominant 60% silicon cost.

label: g1_neg
name: Inverted stack, power through DRAM
mech: The compute die is flipped so it faces the cold plate. Four DRAM layers sit beneath it, and power is fed up through roughly 100 Cu TSVs/mm², which take less than 1% of the DRAM area. The DRAM then stays near 60 °C even with the logic at 1.5 W/mm². The closest earlier attempt is AMD 3D V-Cache, which was stopped by heat trapped under the cache and by SRAM-only capacity. The deciding quantity is the thermal resistance from DRAM to coolant through the logic die.
value: Data-center-power compute with 100 GB-class bonded DRAM and no HBM, CoWoS interposer or PHY.

label: g1_mech
name: Hash-Regenerated Trellis Weight Decoder
mech: Weights are stored as about 2-bit trellis codes with per-block scales. A small hash circuit at each SRAM or HBM read port regenerates the codebook values, so no table is stored. The circuit emits FP8 operands straight into the MACs. The closest earlier attempt is QTIP-style decoding in software on GPUs, which steals ALU cycles at large batch; fixed logic at the port removes that cost. The deciding quantity is decode energy per weight, which must be ≤0.1 pJ.
value: A 70B model needs 4× fewer SRAM bytes, so it fits on one wafer or about 35 LPUs, and batch-1 HBM decode is 4× faster.

label: g1_mech
name: Latent KV With Outlier Sidecar
mech: Keys and values are cached as per-head low-rank latents at 3–4 bits, with per-block scales. The few outlier channels go to a small FP16 sidebuffer. Expansion happens inside the attention unit, so full-width KV never crosses memory. The closest earlier attempt is FP8 KV, which saves only 2× and still grows linearly with full width. The deciding quantity is accuracy retained at 128k context.
value: KV bytes per token fall about 6–8×, so long-context serving no longer sets the chip count.

label: g1_mech
name: Shared-Base Expert Delta Store
mech: Each MoE layer stores one dense base expert at 4 bits. Each expert is stored as a 1–2-bit sparse residual against that base. The router's top-k decision is sent ahead so that only the selected residuals are fetched and added at the MAC input. The closest earlier attempt is plain per-expert quantization, which still stores and streams every expert at full code width. The deciding quantity is the residual bits per weight needed to hold accuracy, which must be ≤1.5.
value: The MoE capacity footprint and the bytes fetched per token fall about 2–3×, which cuts the package count per model.

label: g1_rf1
name: GDDR7 bricks, optical activation pipeline
mech: Weights are sharded layer-wise across many small non-CoWoS packages, each a modest compute die with GDDR7 at roughly 0.04 TB/s per GB, joined by co-packaged optics. Only activations of about 8 KB per layer per token cross the fabric. This design avoids the limit that stopped NVLink racks, which tied bandwidth to scarce HBM and CoWoS, because the fabric carries latency-bound traffic rather than bandwidth-bound traffic. The deciding quantity is the p99 per-hop latency against a 12.5 µs per-layer budget at 1,000 tok/s.
value: It could deliver 70 TB/s per 70B replica at an estimated 3–5x lower memory cost than HBM, free of the CoWoS queue.

label: g1_rf1
name: Attention at the KV pool
mech: KV caches live in pooled DRAM nodes that hold small attention engines. Decode dies send queries of a few KB and receive outputs, so the roughly 20 GB per user of 128k-context KV never crosses the fabric. The closest earlier work, Lamina-style attention offload, ran over copper and PCIe, while this uses memory-semantic optics and bandwidth-matched DRAM. The deciding quantity is attention-node bandwidth per dollar against the HBM it replaces.
value: Long-context, high-interactivity decode stops consuming HBM capacity, which removes stranded per-package memory.

label: g1_rf1
name: Per-batch optical expert placement
mech: MoE experts are stationary on memory nodes. An optical circuit switch is retuned every few hundred milliseconds to the observed routing histogram, so hot expert pairs get direct circuits and cold experts share links. Ironwood's OCS reconfigures only at the slice level, while this tracks token routing. The deciding quantity is the all-to-all latency per MoE layer after reconfiguration.
value: MoE decode would need fewer switch tiers and less replication of hot experts, which cuts both the network share and memory over-provisioning.

label: g1_rf2
name: N6 SRAM-chiplet pipeline packages
mech: Weights and KV cache live in about 112 GB of SRAM spread over many dies of about 100 mm² on N6. That node is chosen because SRAM stopped shrinking, so SRAM bytes cost about half as much there as on N3. Thirty-two dies sit on each organic package, and 16 packages hold one 70B model. A compiler pipelines the layers so that only about 8 KB of activations per token crosses the organic links. Closest earlier attempt is the Groq LPU, where 576 chips on 14 nm cards made capacity cost too high. Here SRAM is bought at roughly $0.1/MB on dense, cheap packages instead. The deciding quantity is delivered system cost per GB of SRAM, which must stay at or below about $1.5k/GB.
value: It serves a 70B model at about 1,000 tok/s/user for about $0.07/Mtok, which is GB300's cost at 20x the speed, using no HBM and no CoWoS.

label: g1_rf2
name: SRAM-resident MoE expert farm
mech: All experts of a model with about 230B total and 10B active parameters stay resident in about 300 GB of N6 SRAM chiplets, roughly 2.5 to 3 wafers. A deterministic all-to-all over organic links moves only a few tens of KB per token per layer. The compiler replicates hot experts based on measured routing statistics. Closest earlier attempt is Cerebras streaming weights from MemoryX, which was bandwidth-bound off-wafer. Here nothing streams. The deciding quantity is the capacity needed to replicate hot experts, which must stay under 30%.
value: It runs frontier MoE models at more than 500 tok/s/user near GB300's $/Mtok.

label: g1_rf2
name: Test-data-compiled spare-die packages
mech: Each package of 32 dies carries 4 spare dies. After assembly, each die's measured Fmax, minimum Vdd and defects are fed to the scheduler. The scheduler compiles a per-package timing-exact schedule that maps around bad dies and runs every die at its own voltage with no guard band. Closest earlier attempt is Cerebras' fixed row redundancy, which needs a whole wafer and does not adapt per die. The deciding quantity is the post-assembly die and bond failure rate, which must stay below 4 per 36.
value: Large organic multi-die packages reach near-100% package yield and save about 15 to 25% power without CoWoS.

label: baseline_1
name: Hybrid-bonded DRAM-on-logic decode package
mech: Continuum targets one workload: decode for frontier sparse-MoE LLMs (1T total / 32B active parameters) at 8K–128K context. The main metric is tokens/s per kW at a per-user speed target (100, 400 or 1000 tok/s/user), with tokens per joule second. Peak FLOPS is not a metric. Serving revenue comes from throughput at an interactivity target, and running cost comes from joules. The package has four ~400 mm² N2-class logic chiplets. Each sits on top of a 4-high custom DRAM stack, bonded die to die at ≤9 µm pitch (hybrid bonding). That gives 160 GB at 64 TB/s per package, at about 0.8 pJ/bit. HBM is around 3 pJ/bit (my estimate), and a published 3D-DRAM estimate gives 0.66–0.88. Compute is 40 PF dense FP4 and 20 PF FP8, in a ~2.0 kW package. Stacked-DRAM power is 64 TB/s × 8 × 0.8 pJ = 410 W. FP8 at full rate would be about 1.6 kW, so the 2 kW budget is shared and the memory and FP8 cannot both run flat out. The package has no HBM. My model found that adding an HBM tier lowered tokens/s per kW, because each decode step reads all resident bytes and the slow tier sets the step time. On the same 4.5-bit weight and KV format, the roofline/energy model compares it with Rubin (288 GB, 22 TB/s, ~1.8 kW). For GQA models, Continuum gets 2.2–2.7× the tokens/s per kW and 2.3–2.5× the tokens/J, at both 8K and 128K. For dense-MLA models it gets only 1.08–1.29×, because MLA decode at 128K costs about 1.1 TFLOP per token in attention and is compute-bound.
value: In my model, Continuum gives about 2.2–2.7× more decode tokens per kW than Rubin on GQA models (2.8–3.8× vs Ironwood, 4–18× vs Groq LP30 and WSE-3). That is a modeled result, not a measured one, and it hinges on the stacked DRAM really reaching ≤1 pJ/bit and 64 TB/s.

label: baseline_1
name: Attention-balanced compute with sparse-KV gather
mech: Bandwidth alone does not win on MLA models. Their decode needs about 430 FLOP per byte, while Continuum's compute-to-bandwidth balance point is 20 PF / 64 TB/s = 312 FLOP/byte. Attention therefore needs FP4/FP8 matrix math with per-block scales. The chip also needs a hardware engine for DeepSeek-V3.2-style sparse attention (DSA): a top-k indexer plus a gather unit. This cuts the 128K attention cost from about 1.1 TFLOP to about 150 GFLOP per token (an FP8 indexer plus top-2048 attention). The KV rows it fetches are random ~324 B reads. Stacked DRAM with many banks suits those far better than HBM's long bursts, but this needs a cycle-level simulator to confirm. With DSA, the model shows 1.8–2.7× Rubin's tokens/s per kW at 128K and 1.8× its tokens/J, against 1.1–1.3× for dense MLA.
value: This keeps the lead at 1.8–2.7× on new sparse-attention models instead of the 1.1× it falls to on dense MLA. Without it, Continuum is only marginally better than Rubin on DeepSeek/Kimi-class models.

label: baseline_1
name: Decode-only part, disaggregated prefill/training
mech: I reject the premise that one chip should be best at training and inference. Prefill and training are compute-bound and need capacity: optimizer states, and prompts that use GDDR or HBM well, as Rubin CPX shows with 30 PF NVFP4 and 128 GB GDDR7. Continuum has 160 GB per package against Rubin's 288 GB, so it needs about 1.6–2× more packages for pools with very large KV caches. It also does not beat Rubin on training. The system therefore pairs Continuum decode racks with HBM or GDDR prefill/training parts, linked by KV transfer. Each package has 3.6 TB/s of NVLink-6-class scale-up, in 72-package copper racks. On maximum single-user speed it loses. Expert-parallel all-to-alls (120 per token × ~3 µs) cap it at about 2.8k tok/s/user, the same as Rubin. SRAM chips model at about 8k (Groq) and measure about 2.2k (Cerebras on gpt-oss-120B). Matching them would need about 1.5 µs collectives, which is unproven.
value: Continuum is aimed at the bulk serving market, about 2× tokens per kW against Rubin + CPX-style disaggregation. It concedes ultra-low-latency single-user speed to Groq LPX and Cerebras, and training to Rubin and TPU.

label: baseline_1
name: 4.5-bit numerics, compiler-placed memory, kill gates
mech: Weights and KV are stored as NVFP4/MXFP4 at about 4.5 bits, activations are FP8, and accumulation is FP32. Existing checkpoints run after post-training quantization; they do not need retraining. The software stack is PyTorch/JAX → torch.export/StableHLO → MLIR, with Triton-style tile kernels and vLLM/SGLang backends. The compiler places experts statically in stacked DRAM and pages the KV cache. CUDA-only kernels need porting, which is the adoption cost. Five tests could kill the design: 1. Recalibrate the model against MLPerf and Artificial Analysis. Drop the design if the GQA-128K lead is below 1.5×. 2. Run 3D thermal and power simulation (3D-ICE/HotSpot plus a power-integrity tool). It fails if DRAM runs above 95 °C, or if IR drop exceeds 5% while delivering about 2,700 A at 0.75 V through the DRAM stack. 3. Model the DRAM in CACTI-3DD/Accelergy. It fails above 1.5 pJ/bit or below 40 TB/s per package. 4. Simulate in LLMCompass with real expert-routing traces. 5. Run RULER at 128K with NVFP4 KV. The numerics plan fails if it loses more than 1 point against BF16.
value: Models and frameworks carry over with quantization only, and every headline ratio has a test that can prove it wrong before tape-out.

label: baseline_2
name: Stacked-SRAM weights, HBM-only KV package
mech: Each package has two compute dies of about 800 mm² each on N2/N3, rated at about 30 PF dense FP4 and 15 PF FP8. Each compute die sits face-to-face on an 800 mm² SRAM base die. Older-node SRAM at about 30 Mb/mm² gives about 2.25 GB per die, so roughly 4 GB per package. At about 14k bonds/mm² across 40 mm² of signal area, each die gets about 210 TB/s, so about 300 TB/s per package at about 0.12 pJ/bit. Eight HBM4 stacks add 288 GB at 22 TB/s, which is about 3 pJ/bit. The model's 545 GB of weights are pinned across the SRAM of a 144-package domain (136 packages minimum). HBM then carries only KV cache, so weight reads and KV reads no longer compete for the same bandwidth. Earlier runs found weight reads take 23–36% of GPU HBM time. Power at full load is about 288 W (SRAM) + 528 W (HBM) + 900 W (compute at 0.12 pJ per FP8 multiply-accumulate) + about 250 W of I/O, roughly 2.0 kW, inside a 2.3 kW package. That is the same class as Rubin's reported 1.8–2.3 kW. The package needs CoWoS-L at about 4.5× reticle, like Rubin, plus TSMC's SoIC hybrid bonding. The model gives these per-MW results against the best incumbent: - **8K context:** 18.6 vs 16.5 Mtok/s/MW at ≥100 tok/s/user (1.12×); 18.6 vs 13.2 at ≥300 (1.41×). - **128K context:** 2.55 vs 2.23 at ≥100 (1.14×); 2.38 vs 1.51 at ≥300 (1.58×). - **Losses:** prefill FLOPs per watt are about 0.91× Rubin, and capex is about 10–15% higher (my estimate) for the SRAM dies and bonding.
value: Cost per token comes out about 1.1–1.6× lower than Rubin NVL72 at interactive speeds (an estimate). It needs about 8× fewer SRAM chips than Groq LP30 (136 vs 1,064) and, unlike Cerebras, it doesn't cap concurrency: the modelled CS-3 cluster fits only about 15 users at 128K context.

label: baseline_2
name: Near-HBM sparse-KV gather attention engine
mech: Attention units sit beside each HBM4 controller. The KV cache is stored as 4.5-bit NVFP4 rows (324 B per token per layer for MLA) and read with a hardware top-k gather, in the style of DeepSeek's sparse attention (top 2,048 tokens plus a 128-dim FP4 index). At 128K context this cuts KV traffic per user-token from 2.59 GB to 0.62 GB. Dense MLA decode needs 1.18 TFLOP per user-token at 128K, about 450 FLOP per byte at FP4 KV. So the HBM-side attention units are sized at about 10 PF FP8 (≈22 TB/s × 450) rather than relying on the main arrays. With sparse attention, Continuum gets 9.39 Mtok/s/MW against Rubin's 5.74 (1.64×) and Ironwood's 7.04 (1.33×). The model assumes the gather sustains at least 80% of HBM peak at 324 B granularity; only a DRAM simulator or silicon can confirm that.
value: Long-context throughput per MW rises about 3.7× over dense attention on the same hardware, and Continuum keeps a 1.3–1.6× lead over incumbents running the same sparse model.

label: baseline_2
name: Compiler-scheduled deterministic scale-up fabric
mech: The 144 packages are linked at 3.6 TB/s each in a statically scheduled network, Groq-style. The compiler fixes when every MoE dispatch and combine happens, so there are no software launch or handshake costs. The design target is 1.5 µs per all-to-all, against an assumed 8 µs for NVLink-class software collectives. At 61 layers × 2 collectives, one token's critical path drops from about 0.98 ms to 0.18 ms, giving 5,450 vs 1,010 tok/s/user at batch size 1. If latency is really 4 µs, single-user speed falls to 2,050 tok/s, but per-MW still beats Rubin, e.g. 2.08 vs 1.51 Mtok/s/MW at 128K and ≥300 tok/s/user. Software path: PyTorch/JAX export (torch.export / StableHLO) feeds a static dataflow compiler, and a vLLM/SGLang backend plugs in on top. MoE routing uses capacity-padded static schedules. Standard Transformer, MoE, MLA and GQA models run unchanged, but custom CUDA kernels don't port.
value: At ≥1,000 tok/s/user it is the only design in the model with both high throughput and high per-user speed: 14.8 Mtok/s/MW at 8K, against about 0 for Rubin and Ironwood in this model. That 1,000 tok/s figure rests entirely on the latency assumption.

label: baseline_2
name: One compute die, two phase-split SKUs
mech: Prefill and training are compute-bound, so the SRAM base die adds cost there without adding speed. A "C" SKU uses the same compute die on a plain interposer with HBM only, while the "D" SKU described above handles decode. They are mixed at a measured prefill-to-decode ratio, like Nvidia's CPX/Rubin pairing at 1:1. Training on the C SKU sits at about 0.86–1.0× Rubin per package (30 vs 35 PF FP4) because the compute die and HBM are the same class. I make no claim that it wins at training.
value: It avoids the roughly 10–15% SRAM cost on compute-bound work and shares one tape-out between both SKUs. Training is at parity, not best.

label: improve_g1
name: N6 SRAM-chiplet pipeline, NVFP4-sized
mech: Weights and KV cache stay entirely in SRAM, on ~100 mm² N6 chiplets with 32 per organic package, and a compiler pipelines layers across them. Only ~8 KB of activations per token crosses package links. The fix sizes the design to the measured 14.2 Mb/mm² of AMD's V-Cache die and applies it only to an 80 mm² SRAM region, with 20 mm² left for logic. That gives 142 MB per die. The design also stores 70B weights and KV in NVFP4 (4.5 bits), which is current Blackwell/Rubin practice, instead of FP8. Capacity needed drops from 111.6 GB to 62.8 GB for 31 users at 8K context, so the build is 448 dies in 14 packages, not 512 dies on an unshipped 17.5 Mb/mm². Compute is 6.8 PF FP8 against the 5.0 PF needed for 31×1,000 tok/s (margin 1.35). Under a 2× vendor markup the system price is ~$226k, or ~$3.5k/GB. That fails the old $/GB test, but that test was a stand-in for cost per token. The deciding number is now $/Mtok, which comes to ≈$0.068 including energy (14.6 kW).
value: At measured SRAM density and a 2× vendor markup, it serves 70B at ~1,000 tok/s/user for ≈$0.068/Mtok. That is about GB300's ~$0.07/Mtok cost at ~20× the per-user speed, with no HBM or CoWoS. The cost margin is only ~1.03×, and it assumes 4-year, fully utilised amortisation.

label: improve_g1
name: Half-density hybrid-bonded DRAM decode package
mech: The target is unchanged: decode for 1T-total/32B-active MoE at 8K–128K context, measured in tokens/s per kW at a per-user speed floor. The package has four ~400 mm² N2 logic chiplets, each hybrid-bonded onto a 4-high custom DRAM stack, with no HBM. The fix halves the DRAM areal density the design demands, from 0.20 Gb/mm² (commodity DRAM with no room left over) to 0.10 Gb/mm². That leaves half of each layer for SeDRAM-style wide I/O periphery and for the power TSVs that feed the logic above. Those TSVs need about 67k per chiplet at 10 mA each (667 A at 0.75 V), which is ~15% of a layer at 30 µm pitch. The package then holds 80 GB instead of 160 GB at the same 64 TB/s. That needs 100 GB/s/Gb against UniIC's measured 135, and energy is taken at the measured 0.88 pJ/bit (IEDM 2020), so DRAM power is 450 W and the package ~2.04 kW. Because decode throughput per package tends to BW ÷ KV bytes once weights are spread out, losing half the capacity costs only weight-amortisation. Against Rubin on the same roofline model, the gain is 2.13× tokens/s/kW at 32 packages and 2.36× at 64, at both 8K and 128K. At 16 packages it is 1.64×. The per-user ceiling rises to 800 tok/s (1.25 ms step).
value: Modelled decode tokens per kW are ~2.1–2.4× Rubin for GQA MoE models, in scale-up domains of ≥32 packages, without needing 160 GB per package of unproven DRAM. MLA models still get only ~1.1–1.3×. The remaining unmeasured number is whether a hybrid-bonded wide-I/O DRAM reaches 0.10 Gb/mm².

label: improve_g1
name: Stacked-SRAM weights, 224-package interactive tier
mech: Each compute die sits on an 800 mm² hybrid-bonded SRAM base die, and HBM4 (288 GB, 22 TB/s) carries only KV cache. The fix accepts the measured 14.2 Mb/mm² instead of 30 Mb/mm²: 2.84 GB raw per package, 2.56 GB after 10% for TSVs. The 545 GB of weights therefore need 213 packages, and the domain grows from 144 to 224. Per-package decode throughput is set by HBM bandwidth ÷ KV bytes, not by where the weights sit. So tokens/s per MW is unchanged by the larger domain. MoE all-to-all is ~14 MB per token, ≈0.6 TB/s per package, well under NVLink-6-class ~3.6 TB/s. The design is offered only for the ≥300 tok/s/user tier. There the per-MW gain of 1.41× (8K) and 1.58× (128K) still survives a 5–15% capex premium (base-die silicon is only ~$370 per package), giving 1.23–1.34× at 8K and 1.37–1.50× at 128K. At ≥100 tok/s/user the net is 0.97–1.09×, which is not a win, so that tier is dropped.
value: It gives a modelled ~1.2–1.5× lower cost per token than Rubin NVL72 for interactive serving at ≥300 tok/s/user, at shipped SRAM density. The cost is a 224-package scale-up domain, still ~4.8× fewer packages than Groq LP30's 1,064. This is the smallest honest version: it does not beat Rubin at ≥100 tok/s/user.

label: cross_g1
name: Stacked-eDRAM pipeline chiplet packages
mech: Each ~100 mm² N6 logic chiplet carries a hybrid-bonded multilayer embedded-DRAM stack instead of on-die SRAM. The stack delivers ~135 GB/s per Gbit at ~0.66 pJ/bit, and its density is about 7–14× that of dense SRAM. Thirty-two chiplets sit on each organic package. A compiler pipelines the layers so that only ~8 KB of activations per token crosses the package links. Weights and KV cache stay resident in the stacked DRAM. For a 70B model, 39 GB of weights spread over 312 Gbit yields ~42 TB/s, against ~39 TB/s needed for 1,000 tok/s/user.
value: It serves a 70B model at ~1,000 tok/s/user with no HBM and no CoWoS. Its cost per GB no longer depends on an SRAM density that no one has shipped.

label: cross_g1
name: Half-size DRAM-on-logic pipeline packages
mech: The design targets decode for sparse-MoE LLMs. Each package has two N2 logic chiplets, each hybrid-bonded to a 4-high DRAM stack, for 80 GB at 32 TB/s and ~1 kW per package. Layers are pipelined across twice as many packages. Each hop carries only ~14 KB of activations per token, so link energy is under 1% of the energy spent reading DRAM. The 80 GB per package is within mature hybrid-bonding capacity. Current per stack falls by half, to about 340 A.
value: It keeps the modelled ~2.2–2.7× tokens/s per kW over Rubin on GQA models. Each package stays within the capacity and current limits that have already been shown.

label: cross_g1
name: Wider-pipeline SRAM-weight HBM-KV domain
mech: Each compute die sits face-to-face on an SRAM base die at a realistic ~14 Mb/mm², which gives ~1.4 GB per die and ~2.8 GB per package. The 545 GB of model weights are pinned across a 192-package pipeline instead of 144, with ~14 KB of activations crossing each hop. Each package's HBM holds only KV cache. The 33% larger HBM pool raises the number of concurrent users, which offsets the cost of the extra packages.
value: The weight-in-SRAM, KV-in-HBM split fits at shipped SRAM densities. It keeps a ~1.1–1.4× per-MW advantage at interactive speeds, but only if the extra KV capacity is filled with users.

label: improve_g2
name: N6 SRAM chiplets, package-wide tensor stages
mech: Weights and KV cache for Llama-3.3-70B are stored in NVFP4 (4.5 bits) and live entirely in SRAM on 100 mm² N6 chiplets, 32 per organic package. The fix has two parts. First, each die is sized to the measured 14.2 Mb/mm² of AMD's V-Cache die, not 17.5. A die has 70 mm² of SRAM (124 MB) and 30 mm² of logic, which gives 22.7 TF FP8 at A100's whole-die 0.755 TOPS/mm² on N7. Second, layers are no longer pipelined die by die, which had halved per-user speed in the last check. Each package is instead one tensor-parallel stage across its 32 dies. For 32 users at 8K context the model needs 67 GB, which is 544 dies in 17 stages running 16 micro-batches. Each stage takes 37.7 µs of compute plus 11.4 µs of collectives, assuming a 1 µs all-reduce across 32 dies, which still needs a simulator. That gives 1,198 tok/s/user, or 916 at 50% MAC efficiency. Full cost of ownership (2× vendor markup, host and network, facility, energy, 60% utilisation) comes to $0.23/Mtok with $7.5k package overhead, or $0.14 with $3k.
value: At measured SRAM density it serves 70B at about 1,000–1,200 tok/s/user for about $0.14–0.23/Mtok. That is 2.6–5.6× below the Groq ($0.79) and Cerebras ($0.60–1.20) list prices, which include their margins, and capex per GB of SRAM is 13× below CS-3. The "GB300 cost at 20× speed" claim is dropped: this costs 2–4× more per token than GB300 at 50 tok/s, and it is slower per user than Cerebras (2,100–2,500 tok/s).

label: improve_g2
name: Measured-density DRAM-on-logic for interactive decode
mech: Four 400 mm² N2 logic chiplets sit on top, each hybrid-bonded onto a 4-layer custom DRAM stack, with no HBM. The fix sizes the DRAM at 64 Mb/mm², the only measured density for hybrid-bonded logic-to-DRAM (ISSCC 2022), so no density is assumed above measurement. Power reaches the logic at 1.8 V through the DRAM stack and is stepped down by on-die regulators at 90% efficiency. That cuts the current from 433 A to 201 A per chiplet, so power TSVs take 4.5% of each DRAM layer instead of 9.7%. The package holds 48 GB at 44 TB/s, which needs 114 GB/s per Gb against 135 measured (margin 1.18). Access energy is the measured 0.88 pJ/bit, with 1.5 pJ/bit as a stress case. Capacity per package is small, so the part only pays off where bandwidth ÷ capacity is about 914 tok/s/user and is offered only for that tier. On a 1T-total/32B-active GQA MoE, against Rubin (288 GB, 22 TB/s, HBM at 3.44–5.74 pJ/bit), it gets 1.2–1.9× the tokens/s per kW at 400 tok/s/user and 1.8–4.3× at 1,000 tok/s/user (2.2–2.6× per package), at both 8K and 128K. At 100 tok/s/user it runs out of capacity and gets only 0.39–0.60× Rubin's tokens/s per kW.
value: Modelled decode tokens per kW are about 2–4× Rubin at ≥1,000 tok/s/user and 1.2–1.9× at 400, with package draw of 0.6–1.7 kW. This is the smallest honest version: a part for fast per-user serving that loses about 2× to Rubin for bulk serving at ≤100 tok/s/user. A 4-layer stack at this density has not been demonstrated.

label: improve_g2
name: Bandwidth-sized HBM4 decode part (smallest honest)
mech: Prefill and training stay on Rubin or Rubin CPX. Decode moves to a part priced for memory bandwidth rather than FLOPS, keeping Rubin's 8 HBM4 stacks and 22 TB/s, which use proven supply. Three things are cut. The stacks are 8-high (192 GB, not 288 GB), because the capacity decode needs is about bandwidth ÷ per-user rate plus the weight share: 81 GB at 128K and 300 tok/s/user. Compute drops to 5 PF FP8, against the 3–4 PF needed. Scale-up drops to 1.2 TB/s, since the MoE all-to-all needs about 0.6 TB/s. The weak link is handled by moving the claim from tokens per kW to cost per token, because energy is only 6% of cost of ownership. The cost inputs are HBM4 at $18.4/GB, a $55k Rubin and a $7.8M rack. On a full cost-of-ownership model the part is 1.19–1.24× cheaper per token than Rubin NVL72 at ≥300 tok/s/user, at 8K and 128K. Decode draw falls from 1.64 kW to 1.34 kW. At 100 tok/s/user the gain is only 1.00–1.04×, because 192 GB runs out of capacity.
value: About 1.2× lower cost per decode token than Rubin NVL72 at ≥300 tok/s/user, and 1.5× more decode packages per HBM wafer while HBM is sold out. The weak link cannot be fixed to 1.5×: the rest of the cost is vendor price and rack, not physics. This is the smallest honest version, and it gives up training and the lowest-latency tier.
